title: Non-reciprocal torques guide self-assembly of active particles into clusters with controllable function
authors: Till Welker, Yukino Fujiya, Holger Stark
abstract: Self-assembly of constituents determines structure formation in the microscopic world. Attractive forces can assemble active particles into colloidal machines, but they do not fix the particles' orientations, which limits control over the machine's function. We demonstrate that non-reciprocal turn-towards torques not only assemble active particles into clusters, without requiring attractive forces, but also link particle orientations to the cluster configuration. Symmetry then dictates whether the cluster is static, rotates, or translates. In small systems, the particle number uniquely determines the stable configuration and function. In larger systems, there are multiple stable configurations with distinct functions, and tuning the torque strength allows us to bias towards the desired function, such as a run-and-tumble motion. Because the interactions driving assembly can be switched on and off, the clusters self-assemble when needed. For such a "just-in-time" self-assembly to be practical, fast assembly is necessary. We show that stochastic resetting, implemented by briefly turning off propulsion and torque, significantly speeds up self-assembly by avoiding slow pathways. Together, our findings demonstrate that non-reciprocal torques can rapidly assemble active particles into colloidal micromachines with controllable function.
summary: The research demonstrates that by introducing non-reciprocal torques to active particles, one can guide their self-assembly into structured clusters whose macroscopic function is controllable. The resulting dynamics are governed by the cluster's geometric symmetry, allowing for programmable behavior like controlled translation or rotation. Furthermore, incorporating stochastic resetting significantly enhances the speed of this functional assembly process.
main_problem: To achieve self-assembly of active particles into functional clusters with controllable function, overcoming limitations related to passive assembly and simple attractive forces.
main_result: Non-reciprocal torques can rapidly assemble active particles into colloidal micromachines whose resulting function (static, rotating, or translating) is dictated by the cluster's symmetry and particle number.
method: The study uses Langevin equations of motion to simulate active particles interacting via steric repulsion and non-reciprocal turn-towards torques. Cluster dynamics are analyzed using Mean Squared Displacement (MSD) and occupation probabilities of metastable states.
model_or_system: The system consists of active colloidal particles in two dimensions, propelled by a constant velocity $v_0$ and subject to an interaction torque $\Gamma_{ij} = \Gamma_0 \hat{n}_i 	imes \hat{r}_{ij}$ when neighbors are close. The dynamics are modeled using coupled equations for position and orientation.
key_observables: Center-of-Mass MSD/MSAD, occupation probabilities ($P_i$) of metastable cluster shapes (e.g., triangle, chevron), transition fluxes ($J_{ij}$), and run times during 'run-and-tumble' motion.
important_parameters: Torque strength ($\Gamma_0$), propulsion velocity ($v_0$), particle number, and the ratio $\Gamma_0/v_0$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on overdamped motion; for small systems, cluster symmetry alone determines function; stochastic resetting is used to accelerate assembly by bypassing kinetic traps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how different symmetries (e.g., point vs. single axis) constrain the resulting directed motion via MSD/MSAD plots. Other figures detail multi-stability in larger clusters and the mechanism of 'run-and-tumble' transitions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model using non-reciprocal torques, analyzes how cluster symmetry dictates macroscopic function (static vs. dynamic), demonstrates control over multiple stable states by tuning torque strength, and finally introduces stochastic resetting to achieve fast, controlled assembly.
why_interesting: This work provides a clear example of how engineered non-equilibrium interactions (torques) can impose complex functional constraints on self-assembled matter, drawing parallels between symmetry principles in condensed matter physics and active matter design.
